claim: Medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) produce and present self-antigens and are essential for the establishment of central tolerance.
source: Medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs), which produce and present self-antigens, are essential for the establishment of central tolerance.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established scientific understanding about mTEC function.

claim: mTEC function is complemented by thymic dendritic cells (DCs) which transfer mTEC-produced self-antigens via cooperative antigen transfer (CAT).
source: Since mTEC numbers are limited, their function is complemented by thymic dendritic cells (DCs), which transfer mTEC-produced self-antigens via cooperative antigen transfer (CAT).
evidence: This statement in the abstract references established knowledge about DC function in the thymus.

claim: CAT is required for effective T cell selection.
source: While CAT is required for effective T cell selection, many aspects remain enigmatic.
evidence: This statement in the abstract references established knowledge about CAT function.

claim: Each subset of thymic DCs preferentially targets a distinct mTEC subset(s) in regards to CAT.
source: Using several relevant Cre-based mouse models that control for the expression of fluorescent proteins, we have found that, in regards to CAT, each subset of thymic DCs preferentially targets a distinct mTEC subset(s).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental data from the study.

claim: XCR1+-activated DC subset represented the most potent subset in CAT.
source: Importantly, XCR1+-activated DC subset represented the most potent subset in CAT.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental data from the study.

claim: Thymic DCs can acquire antigens from more than one mTEC.
source: Interestingly, thymic DCs can also acquire antigens from more than one mTEC, and of these, monocyte-derived dendritic cells (moDCs) were determined to be the most efficient.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental data from the study.

claim: Monocyte-derived dendritic cells (moDCs) are the most efficient DC subset in acquiring antigens from more than one mTEC.
source: Interestingly, thymic DCs can also acquire antigens from more than one mTEC, and of these, monocyte-derived dendritic cells (moDCs) were determined to be the most efficient.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental data from the study.

claim: moDCs represented the most potent DC subset in the acquisition of antigen from other DCs.
source: moDCs also represented the most potent DC subset in the acquisition of antigen from other DCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental data from the study.

claim: Central tolerance operates during T cell development in the thymus and can result in the elimination of self-reactive T cells or deviation to a thymic regulatory T cell (tTreg) lineage.
source: Central tolerance, which operates during T cell development in the thymus, can result in the elimination of self-reactive T cells or deviation to a thymic regulatory T cell (tTreg) lineage (Klein et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement references established knowledge with a citation to Klein et al., 2019.

claim: Immature T cells test their T cell receptor (TCR) for potential self-reactivity through scanning of self-antigens presented by antigen-presenting cells (APCs).
source: The underlying principle of this event compels immature T cells to test their T cell receptor (TCR) for potential self-reactivity through the scanning of self-antigens that are presented by antigen-presenting cells (APCs).
evidence: This statement describes established knowledge about T cell selection.

claim: Thymic epithelial cells (TECs) are central to the T cell selection process.
source: Among all thymic APCs, thymic epithelial cells (TECs) are central to this selection process (Klein et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement references established knowledge with a citation to Klein et al., 2014.

claim: TECs are divided into cortical thymic epithelial cells (cTECs) and medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) based on their localization within the thymus.
source: Based on their localization within the thymus, TECs are generally divided into two major populations: cortical thymic epithelial cells (cTECs) and medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) (Derbinski et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement references established knowledge with a citation to Derbinski et al., 2001.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) revealed an unexpected heterogeneity of mTECs with at least five distinct subsets.
source: Recently, results of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) revealed an unexpected heterogeneity of mTECs with at least five distinct subsets defined by developmental stage, transcription profile, and function (referred to as mTEC-I, -II, -IIIa, IIIb, and Tuft cells) (Baran-Gale et al., 2020; Bornstein et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement references findings from other studies with citations to Baran-Gale et al., 2020; Bornstein et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2018.

claim: mTECs express and present more than 80% of the protein-coding genome.
source: Due to their unique ability to express and present more than 80% of the protein-coding genome, mTECs are well-adapted to serve as a principal self-antigen-producing cellular component of central tolerance (Brennecke et al., 2015; Meredith et al., 2015; Sansom et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement references findings from other studies with citations to Brennecke et al., 2015; Meredith et al., 2015; Sansom et al., 2014.

claim: The autoimmune regulator (Aire) controls the gene expression of a large set of tissue-restricted antigens (TRAs) found only in the immune periphery.
source: This is in part facilitated by the expression of the autoimmune regulator (Aire). Aire controls the gene expression of a large set of tissue-restricted antigens (TRAs) that are found only in the immune periphery (Derbinski et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement references established knowledge with a citation to Derbinski et al., 2001.

claim: Any particular TRA is expressed by only 1–3% of mTECs.
source: Interestingly, an effective display of a complete set of thymically expressed TRAs is achieved by their combinatorial mosaic expression by each mTEC with any particular TRA expressed by only 1–3% of mTECs (Derbinski et al., 2008)
evidence: This statement references findings from another study with a citation to Derbinski et al., 2008.

claim: A single mTEC is capable of expressing up to 300 different TRAs.
source: while a single mTEC is capable of expressing up to 300 different TRAs (Meredith et al., 2015; Sansom et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement references findings from other studies with citations to Meredith et al., 2015; Sansom et al., 2014.

claim: The highest Aire and TRA expression is observed within the mTEC-II stage during mTEC progression.
source: During their progression through mTEC-I, -II, -IIIa, and -IIIb stages, the highest Aire and TRA expression is observed within the mTEC-II stage, historically referred to as mTEChigh.
evidence: This statement describes findings about mTEC development and Aire expression.

claim: mTEC-II cells downregulate Aire expression as they enter pre-post Aire and post-Aire phases, but their TRA protein levels remain high.
source: As mTEC-II cells enter pre-post Aire and post-Aire phases (phase -IIIa and -IIIb, respectively), they downregulate the expression of Aire, although their TRA protein levels remain high, making them available for transfer to other cells (Kadouri et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement references findings from another study with a citation to Kadouri et al., 2020.

claim: The expression of TRA in mTEC-I (mTEClow) is limited.
source: It is noteworthy that the expression of TRA in mTEC-I (also referred to as mTEClow) is limited (Baran-Gale et al., 2020; Bornstein et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement references findings from other studies with citations to Baran-Gale et al., 2020; Bornstein et al., 2018.

claim: TRAs from apoptotic mTECs can be transferred into and indirectly presented to T cells by thymic dendritic cells (DCs) via cooperative antigen transfer (CAT).
source: To overcome this limitation, TRAs from apoptotic mTECs can be transferred into, and indirectly presented to, T cells by thymic dendritic cells (DCs) via the process of cooperative antigen transfer (CAT) (Gallegos and Bevan, 2004; Koble and Kyewski, 2009).
evidence: This statement references established knowledge with citations to Gallegos and Bevan, 2004; Koble and Kyewski, 2009.

claim: CAT is critical for the establishment of central tolerance to mTEC-derived self-antigens.
source: It has been demonstrated that CAT is critical for the establishment of central tolerance to mTEC-derived self-antigens (Lancaster et al., 2019; Perry et al., 2014; Perry et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement references findings from other studies with citations to Lancaster et al., 2019; Perry et al., 2014; Perry et al., 2018.

claim: Thymic DCs can be divided into plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) and classical dendritic cells (cDCs), with cDCs subdivided into cDC1 and cDC2 subsets.
source: In general, thymic DCs can be divided into two major categories: plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) and classical dendritic cells (cDCs), the latter of which can be subdivided into cDC1 and cDC2 subsets (Guilliams et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement references established knowledge with a citation to Guilliams et al., 2014.

claim: DC subsets vary in their capacity to acquire mTEC-derived antigens.
source: Previous studies have shown that these DC subsets vary in their capacity to acquire mTEC-derived antigens (Kroger et al., 2017; Lancaster et al., 2019; Vobořil et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement references findings from other studies with citations to Kroger et al., 2017; Lancaster et al., 2019; Vobořil et al., 2020.

claim: The cDC1 subset strongly acquires GFP antigen from mTEC in an Aire-GFP mouse model.
source: The cDC1 subset has been shown to strongly acquire GFP antigen from mTEC in an Aire-GFP mouse model (Perry et al., 2018)
evidence: This statement references findings from another study with a citation to Perry et al., 2018.

claim: The cDC2 subset robustly acquires mOVA antigen in a RIP-mOVA mouse model.
source: while the cDC2 subset robustly acquired mOVA antigen in a RIP-mOVA mouse model (Lancaster et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement references findings from another study with a citation to Lancaster et al., 2019.

claim: The expression of Aire-driven GFP in the thymus is largely restricted to Aire+ mTECs.
source: Since the expression of Aire-driven GFP and mOVA in the thymus was largely restricted to Aire+ mTECs (Gardner et al., 2008)
evidence: This statement references findings from another study with a citation to Gardner et al., 2008.

claim: The expression of mOVA in the thymus is largely restricted to mTECLow/post-Aire mTECs.
source: and mTECLow/post-Aire mTECs, respectively (Mouri et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement references findings from another study with a citation to Mouri et al., 2017.

claim: Distinct subsets of thymic DCs acquire antigens from distinct subsets of mTECs.
source: it has been inferred that distinct subsets of thymic DCs acquire antigens from distinct subsets of mTECs.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous studies mentioned in the text.

claim: scRNAseq analysis exposed a much broader heterogeneity of DCs in the thymus of mice and humans.
source: However, our recent scRNAseq analysis, along with data from the human thymus cell atlas study, exposed a much broader heterogeneity of DCs in the thymus of mice and humans (Park et al., 2020; Vobořil et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement references findings from studies with citations to Park et al., 2020; Vobořil et al., 2020.

claim: Foxn1CreRosa26TdTOM (Foxn1Cre) mice express TdTOM in all populations of CD45–EpCAM+ TECs.
source: we generated (i) Foxn1CreRosa26TdTOM (Foxn1Cre) mice that express TdTOM in all populations of CD45–EpCAM+ TECs (Gordon et al., 2007; Vobořil et al., 2020)
evidence: This describes the experimental mouse model used in the study with supporting citations.

claim: CsnbCreRosa26TdTOM (CsnbCre) mice have Casein β (Csnb) loci operating as an Aire-independent TRA that confines TdTOM expression to the mTECHigh subset and their closest progenitors and progeny.
source: (ii) CsnbCreRosa26TdTOM (CsnbCre) with Casein β (Csnb) loci operating as an Aire-independent TRA that confines TdTOM expression to the mTECHigh subset and their closest progenitors and progeny (Bornstein et al., 2018; Tykocinski et al., 2010)
evidence: This describes the experimental mouse model used in the study with supporting citations.

claim: Defa6iCreRosa26TdTOM (Defa6iCre) represents the 'classical' Aire-dependent TRA model, in which TdTOM is expressed in 1–3% of Aire+ mTECHigh cells as well as post-Aire mTEC progeny.
source: and (iii) Defa6iCreRosa26TdTOM (Defa6iCre). The latter model represents the 'classical' Aire-dependent TRA model, in which TdTOM is expressed in 1–3% of Aire+ mTECHigh cells as well as post-Aire mTEC progeny (Adolph et al., 2013; Dobeš et al., 2015; Figure 1a–c).
evidence: This describes the experimental mouse model used in the study with supporting citations.

claim: The frequency of TdTOM+ cells in the Foxn1Cre model reaches nearly 100%.
source: A comparative analysis of the percentage of TdTOM+ cells within the parent TEC population confirmed that whereas the frequency of TdTOM+ cells in the Foxn1Cre model reached as expected nearly 100%
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis.

claim: The frequency of TdTOM+ cells dramatically decreases in the CsnbCre model compared to Foxn1Cre.
source: it dramatically decreased in the CsnbCre and to a greater extent in the Defa6iCre model (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: The major contribution to the TdTOM+ pool of cells in the CsnbCre and Defa6iCre models comes from the mTECHigh and pre-post Aire subsets.
source: It is also clear that the major contribution to the TdTOM+ pool of cells in the CsnbCre and Defa6iCre models came from the mTECHigh and pre-post Aire subsets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: TdTOM is mostly acquired by CD11c+ cells.
source: As previously shown (Vobořil et al., 2020) as well as in Figure 2b and c, TdTOM is mostly acquired by CD11c+ cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data with reference to previous work and figures.

claim: TdTOM positivity is observed in ~6% of CD11c+ cells in the Foxn1Cre model.
source: Whereas TdTOM positivity was observed in ~6% of CD11c+ cells in the Foxn1Cre model
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: TdTOM positivity in CsnbCre is limited to ~0.6% of CD11c+ cells.
source: its frequency in CsnbCre and Defa6iCre was limited to ~0.6% and ~0.02%, respectively (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's experimental data with reference to a figure.

claim: TdTOM positivity in Defa6iCre is limited to ~0.02% of CD11c+ cells.
source: its frequency in CsnbCre and Defa6iCre was limited to ~0.6% and ~0.02%, respectively (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's experimental data with reference to a figure.

claim: The ratio between the frequency of TdTOM+CD11c+ and TdTOM+CD45–EpCAM+ TECs is comparable across Foxn1Cre, CsnbCre, and Defa6iCre mouse models.
source: Interestingly, since the frequency of TdTOM+ TECs was analogously decreased across the Foxn1Cre, CsnbCre, and Defa6iCre mouse models (Figure 1c), the ratio between the frequency of TdTOM+CD11c+ and TdTOM+CD45–EpCAM+ TECs was comparable (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis with reference to figures.

claim: CAT efficiency between donor TECs and CD11c+ APC acceptors is similar irrespective of the robustness and cell-subset range of TdTOM expression in TECs.
source: These analyses argue for the similarity in CAT efficiency between donor TECs and CD11c+ APC acceptors, irrespective of the robustness and cell-subset range of TdTOM expression in TECs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from the study.

claim: XCR1+ aDCs are the most efficient cells involved in CAT irrespective of the Cre-based Rosa26TdTOM model used.
source: A comparative analysis of the ability of each of these thymic CD11c+ APC subsets to acquire TEC-derived TdTOM showed that XCR1+ aDCs were the most efficient cells involved in CAT irrespective of the Cre-based Rosa26TdTOM model used.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis.

claim: Macs and pDCs are relatively inefficient in CAT.
source: On the other hand, while Macs and pDCs were relatively inefficient, the remaining subsets varied in this efficiency depending on the Cre-model analyzed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: TdTOM is transferred from TECs to all subpopulations of thymic CD11c+ APCs and is not endogenously expressed by these APCs.
source: Using bone marrow (BM) chimeras of sublethally irradiated mouse models (Foxn1Cre, CsnbCre, and Defa6iCre) reconstituted with congenically marked BM cells isolated from WT animals, we verified that TdTOM is indeed transferred from TECs to all subpopulations of thymic CD11c+ APCs and is not endogenously expressed by these APCs themselves (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–f).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data using bone marrow chimeras with reference to figures.

claim: The contribution of cDC1s and moDCs to CAT is robust in all three Cre-based Rosa26TdTOM models.
source: Analyzing each of the Cre-based Rosa26TdTOM mouse models individually (Figure 2f), the data revealed that whereas the contribution of cDC1s and moDCs to CAT was robust in all three models
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: The contribution of pDCs, Macs, cDC2s, and both populations of aDC subsets to CAT varies among the Cre-based Rosa26TdTOM models.
source: the contribution of pDCs, Macs, cDC2s, and both populations of aDC subsets varied among the models.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis.

claim: The ratio between the percentage of TdTOM+ DC subset and the overall percentage for cDC2s, pDCs, and Macs is increased in the Foxn1Cre mouse model.
source: Notably, the ratio between the percentage of TdTOM+ DC subset and the overall percentage for cDC2s, pDCs, and Macs was increased in the Foxn1Cre mouse model.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis.

claim: The ratio for XCR1+ and XCR1– aDCs is lowest in Foxn1Cre, increases in CsnbCre, and is highest in the Defa6iCre model.
source: In contrast, this ratio for XCR1+ and XCR1– aDCs was the lowest in Foxn1Cre, with an increase detected in CsnbCre, and the highest ratio detected in the Defa6iCre model (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: CAT to cDC1s significantly correlates with the expression of TdTOM in mTECHigh.
source: Specifically, CAT to cDC1s significantly correlated with the expression of TdTOM in mTECHigh
evidence: This is a finding from the study's linear regression analysis.

claim: CAT to XCR1+ aDCs correlates with mTECHigh, pre-post Aire, and Tuft mTECs.
source: XCR1+ aDCs with mTECHigh, pre-post Aire, and Tuft mTECs
evidence: This is a finding from the study's linear regression analysis.

claim: CAT to XCR1– aDCs correlates with mTECHigh and pre-post Aire mTECs.
source: whereas XCR1– aDCs with mTECHigh and pre-post Aire mTECs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's linear regression analysis.

claim: pDCs and Macs correlate with antigen production in post-Aire mTECs.
source: Interestingly, pDCs, and to a lesser extent Macs, correlated with antigen production in post-Aire mTECs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's linear regression analysis.

claim: The positive correlation between pDCs and post-Aire mTECs is consistent with Hassall's corpuscles affecting the migration and activation of thymic pDCs through the production of chemokines and cytokines.
source: The positive correlation observed between pDCs and post-Aire mTECs is consistent with the fact that Hassall's corpuscles affect the migration and activation of thymic pDCs through the production of chemokines and cytokines (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in the context of previous research with a citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claim: Macs, cDC2s, and pDCs correlate with the mTECLow population.
source: Macs, cDC2s, and pDCs were found to also correlate with the mTECLow population.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's linear regression analysis.

claim: The Macs population and cDC2s significantly correlate with the expression of TdTOM in cTECs.
source: In addition, the Macs population, and to a lesser extent cDC2s, significantly correlated with the expression of TdTOM in cTECs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's linear regression analysis.

claim: Thymic Macs and cDC2s reside in the thymic cortex.
source: This is consistent with the notion that both thymic Macs and cDC2s reside in the thymic cortex (Baba et al., 2009; Breed et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement references established knowledge with citations to Baba et al., 2009; Breed et al., 2019.

claim: CAT to pDCs, Macs, and cDC2s is highly affected by the frequency of total TdTOM+ TECs.
source: It is also important to emphasize that CAT to pDCs, Macs, and cDC2s is highly affected by the frequency of total TdTOM+ TECs (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: If the availability of TEC-derived antigens is limited, pDCs, Macs, and cDC2s are outcompeted in CAT by other DC subsets.
source: Thus, if the availability of TEC-derived antigens is limited, these subsets are outcompeted in CAT by other DC subsets.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: CAT occurs between subsets of TECs and thymic DCs in a selective manner, with the exception of moDCs.
source: Together, this data confirms the hypothesis that CAT occurs between subsets of TECs and thymic DCs in a selective manner, with the exception of moDCs, which failed to reveal a preference for any subset of TECs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's experimental data analysis.

claim: moDCs failed to reveal a preference for any subset of TECs in CAT.
source: Together, this data confirms the hypothesis that CAT occurs between subsets of TECs and thymic DCs in a selective manner, with the exception of moDCs, which failed to reveal a preference for any subset of TECs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis.

claim: Most thymic CD11c+ subsets acquire antigens from more than one mTEC subset.
source: In experiments in which single-fluorescent protein (FP) transfer mouse models were utilized, most of the thymic CD11c+ subsets acquired antigens from more than one mTEC subset (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: GFP expression is absent in TECs isolated from Foxn1CreConfettiBrainbow2.1 mice.
source: Visualizing TECs from Foxn1CreConfettiBrainbow2.1 and MHCII-EGFP mice, the latter used as a positive control, either separately or as a mixed cell suspension, confirmed that GFP is indeed absent in TECs isolated from Foxn1CreConfettiBrainbow2.1 mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data with reference to a figure.

claim: TECs that express YFP do not express RFP and/or CFP and vice versa in Foxn1CreConfettiBrainbow2.1 mice.
source: Given that YFP and RFP/CFP are expressed from mutually exclusive cassettes in Foxn1CreConfettiBrainbow2.1 mice (Snippert et al., 2010), those TECs that express YFP do not express RFP and/or CFP and vice versa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b–d).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data with reference to a citation and figures.

claim: DCs that are positive for both RFP and YFP must have obtained these antigens from two or more distinct TECs.
source: Therefore, those DCs that were positive for both RFP and YFP must have obtained these antigens from two or more distinct TECs (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental design and data with reference to a figure.

claim: Multi-antigen transfer occurs nearly as frequently as the transfer from a single mTEC.
source: We found that this multi-antigen transfer occurred nearly as frequently as the transfer from a single mTEC and that all CD11c+ APCs were involved in repetitive CAT.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis.

claim: All CD11c+ APCs are involved in repetitive CAT.
source: We found that this multi-antigen transfer occurred nearly as frequently as the transfer from a single mTEC and that all CD11c+ APCs were involved in repetitive CAT.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis.

claim: moDCs reveal the highest frequency of RFP+YFP+ cells, suggesting a high level of promiscuity in targeting TEC subsets.
source: However, moDCs revealed the highest frequency of RFP+YFP+ cells, which suggests a high level of promiscuity in targeting TEC subsets (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis with reference to figures.

claim: The transfer of CFP membrane antigen is observed less frequently than that of cytosolic antigens YFP and RFP.
source: The Foxn1CreConfettiBrainbow2.1 model also showed that the transfer of the CFP membrane antigen was observed less frequently than that of cytosolic antigens YFP and RFP.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis.

claim: CFP transfer is largely mediated by XCR1+ aDCs, which exhibit more than a fivefold higher frequency of CFP positivity than any other CD11c+ subset.
source: CFP transfer was largely mediated by XCR1+ aDCs, which exhibited more than a fivefold higher frequency of CFP positivity than any other CD11c+ subset (Figure 4c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis with reference to figures.

claim: The highest frequency of CFP+RFP+YFP+ cells is found in the moDC subset.
source: As expected and consistent with their strong capacity to acquire FPs from more than one mTEC, the highest frequency of CFP+RFP+YFP+ cells was found in the moDC subset (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g, right plot).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: CFP is localized mainly to the plasma membranes of CAT-experienced XCR1+ aDCs.
source: It is of note that CFP was in direct contrast to other FPs that were localized mainly to the plasma membranes of CAT-experienced XCR1+ aDCs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's imaging flow cytometry analysis.

claim: A single CD11c+ APC frequently acquires antigens from more than one mTEC.

claim: moDCs are the most potent subset in repetitive CAT.
source: and that the most potent subset in this repetitive CAT were moDCs.

claim: XCR1+ aDCs are effective in the acquisition of both cytosolic and membrane-bound antigens.
source: Moreover, we also showed that XCR1+ aDCs were effective in the acquisition of both cytosolic and membrane-bound antigens.

claim: Out of all CD45.1+CD11c+ cells, approximately 0.75% acquire TdTOM from CD45.2+CD11c+ cells in mixed BM chimera experiments.

claim: The contribution of both aDC subsets and cDC2s to CAT from other CD11c+ cells is robust.

claim: The highest frequency of TdTOM+ cells from other CD11c+ cells is found among the moDC subset.
source: the highest frequency of TdTOM+ cells was found among the moDC subset (Figure 5d, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's bone marrow chimera experiment with reference to figures.

claim: Thymic CD11c+ cells, especially moDCs, acquire antigens from other CD11c+ cells.
source: Thus, thymic CD11c+ cells, especially moDCs, acquired antigens not only from TECs but from other CD11c+ cells as well.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's bone marrow chimera experiment.

claim: CAT is mediated predominantly by preferential pairing between cTECs and Mac and cDC2.

source: (iii) mTECHigh to XCR1+ and XCR1– aDC, and cDC1

source: (iv) pre-post Aire mTEC to XCR1+ and XCR1– aDC

claim: CAT is mediated predominantly by preferential pairing between post-Aire mTEC and pDCs and Mac.
source: (v) post-Aire mTEC to pDCs and Mac

claim: Antigen acquisition by Macs, cDC2s, and pDCs can occur when antigen is abundant.
